stages.title: Computational aerodynamics
stages.hook: Wind tunnels are expensive and slow, yet designers now test hundreds of wing shapes before building a single model. How can a computer predict the flow around a wing, and how do we know it is right?
explain: Aerodynamics is governed by the Navier-Stokes equations: conservation of mass, momentum and energy for a viscous fluid. They have no general closed-form solution, so computational fluid dynamics (CFD) divides the flow into small cells (a mesh) and solves discrete equations, for example with the finite-volume method. Faster approximate methods exist too: thin airfoil theory gives C_L = 2π(α − α₀) for a thin airfoil at small angle of attack, and panel methods solve potential flow around a surface.

Turbulence cannot be fully resolved at practical Reynolds numbers, so industry mostly uses Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) with a turbulence model, while large-eddy simulation (LES) resolves large eddies and models small ones. Near walls, the first cell height is chosen for a target y⁺ = y u_τ ÷ ν. Explicit time-stepping must obey the Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (CFL) condition: CFL = (|u| + a)Δt ÷ Δx ≤ 1 for stability.

Credibility rests on verification (are we solving the equations correctly? grid convergence, order of accuracy) and validation (are we solving the right equations? comparison with experiments). For a scheme of order p, halving the cell size reduces discretisation error by about 2^p. Differences between turbulence models are often the dominant uncertainty at stall and with separation.

example.q: A first-order-in-time explicit solver has Δx = 0.01 m and the largest signal speed |u| + a = 440 m/s. What is the largest stable time step for CFL = 1?

analogies.city: Traffic simulations track thousands of cars with small time steps; a step that is too large lets cars jump through each other.
analogies.sea: A weather and ocean model divides the sea into grid boxes and steps forward in time.
analogies.tech: Rendering an animation frame by frame: too coarse a mesh or step gives a wrong picture.
analogies.music: Sampling sound: if the sampling rate is too low, the waveform is misrepresented.

stages.mnemonic: Mesh it, model turbulence, step within CFL, then verify and validate.
terms: Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes, time-averaged equations with a turbulence model.
Non-dimensional distance from the wall used to size the first mesh cell.
Ratio of the distance a signal travels in one time step to the cell size.
Checking the equations are solved correctly.

misc.wrong: A colourful CFD picture is proof that the answer is correct.
misc.right: CFD results must be verified (mesh and numerical convergence) and validated against experiment. A converged solution can still be wrong if the model is inadequate.

stages.limits: RANS models struggle with strongly separated and unsteady flows, and LES or direct simulation at flight Reynolds numbers is very costly. Thin airfoil theory is valid only for small angles and thin sections.

trip.prompt: Find the section on verification and validation. What is the difference?

questions.q: Which statement best distinguishes verification from validation?
o: Verification checks the equations are solved correctly; validation checks the model matches reality
They are the same thing, only named differently by two groups
Verification uses experiments, while validation only uses computational meshes
Validation is done before any code exists, verification after the first flight
questions.why: Verification is about solving the equations right; validation is about solving the right equations.

questions.q: A solution changes noticeably when the mesh is refined. What does this indicate?
o: It is not yet grid-converged
The solution is already perfect and needs no further checking
Turbulence is completely absent from the flow
The CFL number is exactly zero in the solver
questions.why: A converged answer should change little with refinement.

questions.q: What do turbulence models do in RANS?
o: Represent the effect of turbulent fluctuations on the mean flow
Remove viscosity from the equations entirely so the flow is inviscid
Skip the mesh and solve the flow at a single point
Force the whole flow to stay laminar at all speeds
questions.why: Averaging creates extra stress terms that must be modelled.

questions.q: Why does a time step above the CFL limit make an explicit solver blow up?
o: Information travels further than one cell per step, which the scheme cannot represent
The air runs out of the cells near the wall in each step
The mesh is too fine, so the cells hold no air at all
The time becomes negative inside the loop of the solver
questions.why: The numerical domain of dependence must include the physical one.

questions.q: Which method is cheapest and works for thin airfoils at small angles?
o: Thin airfoil theory
Direct numerical simulation
Wind-tunnel testing
LES
questions.why: Analytical thin airfoil theory is cheap but limited.

questions.q: Thin airfoil theory gives C_L = 2π(α − α₀). For a symmetric airfoil (α₀ = 0) at α = 5° (0.08727 rad), what is C_L to 2 decimals?
First cell height for y⁺ = 1: y = y⁺ν/u_τ. With ν = 1.46×10⁻⁵ m²/s and u_τ = 2 m/s, what is y in micrometres?
A second-order scheme has a discretisation error of 4×10⁻³ on a mesh. When the cell size is halved, what is the expected error in units of 10⁻³?
questions.why: Error ∝ h², so halving h divides it by 4: 4×10⁻³ ÷ 4 = 1×10⁻³.

questions.q: Put these CFD steps in order.
questions.why: A CFD study moves from set-up through meshing and solving to checking.

questions.q: A CFD result for a wing near stall disagrees with wind-tunnel data. List two possible sources of the error.
questions.model: The turbulence model may be inadequate for separated flow and the mesh may be too coarse. Boundary conditions, transition modelling, or the tunnel itself (walls, model deflection) can also contribute.
questions.why: Errors come from both modelling and numerical sources, and from the experiment.

panel.q: A team halves the mesh size and the answer barely changes, but a wind tunnel gives a 10% different drag. Which conclusion is best?
o: The numerics are probably converged, so the difference may come from the model or experiment
The CFD code is wrong in every case, because the tunnel disagrees with it
The tunnel is always right, so the simulation should be thrown away
Mesh refinement is useless, so a finer mesh would not have helped
panel.why: Grid convergence only verifies the numerics; validation differences point to modelling or experimental uncertainty.

panel.q: Why is the CFL limit sometimes avoided with implicit schemes?
o: Implicit schemes can be stable at larger time steps, at a higher cost per step
Implicit schemes do not use time, so the limit has no meaning for them
Implicit schemes never converge, so they ignore the limit
Implicit schemes skip the mesh and solve the flow directly
panel.why: Implicit methods solve coupled equations each step and are less restricted by CFL.

panel.q: Why is it not enough for the designer to trust a single CFD run?
panel.model: Any single run has numerical error and model error. Designers check mesh convergence, compare against experiments and quantify uncertainty before trusting it.
panel.why: Credibility requires verification, validation and uncertainty quantification.

teach.topic: How CFD predicts airflow and how we trust it
teach.model: CFD breaks the air into many small cells and solves the flow equations in each. Turbulence has to be modelled, and the time step must be small enough for the numerical scheme to be stable. To trust the result engineers refine the mesh to see it converge and compare with experiments.

stages.title: Aircraft aeroelasticity
stages.hook: In 1940 a long suspension bridge twisted itself apart in a moderate wind, and aircraft wings can do something related. Why can airflow and a flexible structure together become unstable?
explain: Aeroelasticity studies the interaction of aerodynamic, elastic and inertial forces. Static aeroelasticity includes divergence: lift acting ahead of the elastic axis twists the wing nose-up, increasing the angle of attack, which increases lift and twist. For a simple typical section, the twist grows without limit when the dynamic pressure reaches q_D = K_θ ÷ (e S C_Lα), where K_θ is the torsional stiffness, e the distance of the aerodynamic centre ahead of the elastic axis, S the area and C_Lα the lift curve slope.

Dynamic aeroelasticity includes flutter, a self-excited oscillation in which energy is extracted from the airflow each cycle. Flutter typically couples bending and torsion modes, and it appears above a critical speed that depends on stiffness, mass distribution and the separation of modal frequencies. Flutter can destroy a wing within seconds, so aircraft must show a safe margin (commonly 15% on speed) beyond the flight envelope.

Designers raise flutter speed by increasing stiffness, adding mass balance (moving the centre of mass forward), and tuning frequency separation. Control surfaces can also flutter and are mass-balanced. Testing includes ground vibration tests and flight flutter tests that approach the boundary carefully with measured damping.

example.q: A wing section has K_θ = 2.0×10⁵ N·m/rad, e = 0.2 m, S = 10 m², C_Lα = 5 per rad. Find the divergence speed at sea level (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³).

analogies.music: A violin string excited by a bow gains energy each cycle, a self-excited oscillation like flutter.
analogies.sea: A flag flaps in a steady wind because the flow and cloth drive each other.
analogies.sport: Pushing a swing at the right moment adds energy each cycle.
analogies.city: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge failed from aeroelastic effects in 1940.

stages.mnemonic: Divergence: twist feeds lift feeds twist. Flutter: modes couple and the air feeds the oscillation.
terms: Static instability where twist and aerodynamic load grow each other.
Self-excited oscillation extracting energy from the airflow.
The line through a wing along which a load causes bending but no twist.
Moving mass forward of the hinge or elastic axis to raise flutter speed.
The natural frequency of a vibration mode.

misc.wrong: Flutter happens because of turbulence shaking the wing.
misc.right: Flutter is a self-excited instability at a critical speed. It would occur in smooth air once speed exceeds that critical value.

stages.limits: The typical-section model is a two-degree-of-freedom simplification. Real wings need finite element and unsteady aerodynamic models, and certification includes tests.

trip.prompt: Find the Collar triangle. Which three types of force does it connect?

questions.q: What does the Collar triangle illustrate?
o: Aeroelasticity as the interaction of aerodynamic, elastic and inertial forces
Engine cycles as the interaction of heat, work and pressure
Orbital transfers as the interaction of burns and gravity
Weather forecasting as the interaction of fronts and winds
questions.why: Collar's triangle shows the three kinds of force and the phenomena at their interactions.

questions.q: What makes divergence a static instability?
o: It does not involve oscillation; the twist just grows
It is an oscillation, so it is a dynamic instability
It occurs only in engines, never on wings
It needs turbulence in the air to start
questions.why: Divergence is a monotonic growth of twist, unlike flutter.

questions.q: How does moving the wing's mass forward (mass balancing) help?
o: It reduces coupling between bending and torsion and raises flutter speed
It reduces lift on the wing, so the wing flutters less
It adds drag, which damps the motion of the wing
It changes the density of the air that flows over the wing
questions.why: Mass balancing moves the centre of gravity toward the elastic axis, reducing inertial coupling.

questions.q: Why are swept-back flexible wings prone to a changing effective angle of attack when they bend?
o: Bending a swept wing upward reduces the local angle of attack of the tips (washout), changing load
Sweep removes lift from the wing so it cannot bend upward
Sweep doubles the air density near the wing tips and so changes the load
Bending a swept wing makes the air around it stop flowing
questions.why: Bending-torsion coupling in swept wings changes the local incidence, which can help or hinder.

questions.q: Why does the flight envelope need a margin below the predicted flutter speed?
o: Analyses and tests have uncertainty and flutter can be abrupt and catastrophic
Flutter is harmless, so the margin is just a formality
To make aircraft slower for no good engineering reason
Flutter only occurs below about 100 m/s and so can be ignored
questions.why: Margins cover model error, damage and variation in mass.

questions.q: A wing section has K_θ = 2.0×10⁵ N·m/rad, e = 0.2 m, S = 10 m², C_Lα = 5 per rad. What is the divergence dynamic pressure q_D in pascals?
For q_D = 20 000 Pa and ρ = 1.225 kg/m³, what is the divergence speed in m/s?
A structural mode has stiffness k = 4×10⁶ N/m and mass m = 1000 kg. What is its natural frequency f = (1/2π)√(k/m) in hertz?
Match each phenomenon to its type.
pairs: Loss of control effectiveness due to flexibility
questions.why: Aeroelastic phenomena are classified as static or dynamic.

questions.q: Explain why flutter is called a self-excited oscillation.
questions.model: Flutter needs no external periodic force. The wing's own motion changes the aerodynamic loads in such a way that energy is taken from the airflow during each cycle, so the oscillation grows if damping is less than that energy input.
questions.why: Self-excitation means the oscillation sustains itself via the airflow.

panel.q: A wing's torsional stiffness is doubled with other parameters fixed. By what factor does the divergence speed change?
o: 4 times larger
panel.why: q_D ∝ K_θ and v ∝ √q.

panel.q: A pilot flying a certified aircraft at the maximum design speed notices a growing vibration. What is the best response?
o: Reduce speed immediately
Increase speed
Ignore it
Pull the nose up sharply
panel.why: Reducing speed moves away from the flutter boundary. (Educational statement, not pilot training.)

panel.q: Why do designers put flutter margin on equivalent airspeed rather than altitude?
panel.model: Aerodynamic forces scale with dynamic pressure q = ½ρv², which is what equivalent airspeed represents. Flutter depends on q relative to structural stiffness, so margins are defined in terms of q or equivalent airspeed.
panel.why: Flutter boundaries are functions of dynamic pressure and Mach number.

teach.model: A flexible wing twists under load, and the twist changes the load. In divergence the twist keeps growing with no oscillation above a critical dynamic pressure. In flutter, bending and twisting couple and the airflow feeds energy into the oscillation. Designers keep a safety margin and raise stiffness or mass balance.

points.ask: What makes a wing flexible loads change?
What is divergence?
What is flutter?
How do designers prevent them?

stages.title: Transonic and supersonic flight
stages.hook: Aircraft designers narrow the fuselage near the wing (the 'Coke bottle') and sweep the wing back. How do these odd shapes reduce drag near the speed of sound?
explain: Near Mach 1 local flow over the wing exceeds the speed of sound while the aircraft is still subsonic. The drag-divergence Mach number is where wave drag rises sharply. Sweep reduces the effective Mach number normal to the leading edge: M_eff = M cos Λ. Supercritical airfoils are flat on top to delay and weaken shocks. The area rule says wave drag depends on how the cross-sectional area of the whole aircraft varies along its length, so the fuselage is narrowed where the wing adds area.

In supersonic flow, disturbances propagate within a Mach cone with half-angle μ = arcsin(1/M). Linear (Ackeret) theory gives C_L = 4α ÷ √(M² − 1) and wave drag coefficient C_D,w = 4α² ÷ √(M² − 1) for a thin flat plate at small α. Across a normal shock at M₁ = 2, stagnation pressure falls to 72% of its upstream value (p₀₂/p₀₁ ≈ 0.721), so shocks cost efficiency; oblique shocks cost less, which is why supersonic inlets use ramps.

Supersonic flight has other consequences: sonic booms from the shock waves reaching the ground, aerodynamic heating (the total temperature rises as T₀ = T(1 + 0.2M²)), and the need for engines that slow the air to subsonic speed before the compressor. Concorde cruised near Mach 2 and needed a long runway and high fuel use.

example.q: A swept wing with Λ = 35° flies at M = 0.85. Find the effective Mach number normal to the leading edge.

analogies.sea: A fast motorboat's wake forms a V whose angle narrows as the boat speeds up, like the Mach cone.
analogies.sport: A whip cracking creates a small shock wave.
analogies.city: Squeezing a crowd through a gap: the narrowest section controls the flow, like the area rule.
analogies.tech: Supersonic inlets use ramps to slow flow through a series of weak shocks.

stages.mnemonic: Sweep it back, smooth the area, slow with oblique shocks.
terms: The Mach number where wave drag rises rapidly.
Wave drag follows the smoothness of the total cross-section area distribution.
μ = arcsin(1/M), the half-angle of the Mach cone.
Airfoil with a flat top that weakens shocks.
Pressure signature from shock waves reaching the ground.

misc.wrong: A sonic boom happens only at the moment an aircraft breaks the sound barrier.
misc.right: A supersonic aircraft continuously carries its shock waves with it, so the boom sweeps along the whole ground track while flight remains supersonic.

stages.limits: Ackeret theory applies to thin, low-angle shapes away from Mach 1. Transonic flow is nonlinear and needs CFD or wind-tunnel data.

trip.prompt: Find the picture of an aircraft with a 'waisted' fuselage. Where is the narrowest part?

questions.q: Why are wings swept for high subsonic flight?
o: They lower the Mach number normal to the leading edge and delay wave drag
They increase lift at low speed and so are good for landing
They reduce the weight of the wing to nearly zero
They create more shock waves to carry the load
questions.why: Only the velocity component normal to the leading edge governs compressibility effects.

questions.q: What does the area rule recommend?
o: Smooth variation of total cross-sectional area along the length
Make the fuselage widest where the wing joins the body
Use only one wing so the area stays small
Add a second tail to balance the area
questions.why: Narrowing the fuselage where the wing adds area gives a smoother area distribution.

questions.q: A normal shock at M₁ = 2 is replaced by several weaker oblique shocks in an inlet. What is the benefit?
o: Less total pressure loss
More drag, because several shocks stack up in the inlet
Less thrust, because the engine receives less air
No change, since the shocks make no difference to the pressure
questions.why: Oblique shocks are closer to isentropic compression than a single normal shock.

questions.q: The Mach cone half-angle gets smaller as the Mach number increases. Why?
o: μ = arcsin(1/M), so a larger M gives a smaller angle
μ is fixed by the shape of the aircraft and does not change
Sound speeds up as the aircraft goes faster, narrowing the cone
The aircraft shrinks as it goes faster, so the cone narrows
questions.why: At higher speed the body outruns the waves more, making a narrower cone.

questions.q: Why did Concorde need to manage high skin temperatures at Mach 2?
o: Air brought to rest near the surface heats to the stagnation temperature
The Sun was hotter at that altitude and heated the skin directly
The engines overheated the wings from the inside
Gravity was higher at that altitude and added friction
questions.why: T₀ = T(1 + 0.2M²) is about 1.8T at Mach 2.

questions.q: A swept wing with Λ = 35° flies at M = 0.85 (cos 35° = 0.8192). What is the effective Mach number normal to the leading edge, to 2 decimals?
At M = 2, what is the Mach cone half-angle in degrees?
Ackeret theory: C_L = 4α/√(M² − 1). For α = 2° (0.03491 rad) at M = 2, what is C_L to 3 decimals?
Put these flow states in order of increasing Mach number.
questions.why: These regimes run from M < 0.8, to 0.8–1.2, to above 1.2 and above 5.

questions.q: Explain why a supersonic aircraft's inlet must slow the air to subsonic speed before the compressor.
questions.model: Compressor blades are designed for subsonic relative flow. Supersonic air entering would cause strong shocks, loss and instability, so the inlet slows the flow, through a series of shocks and diffusion, to subsonic speed before it reaches the compressor.
questions.why: Engines need subsonic flow at the compressor face.

panel.q: A fighter doubles its Mach number from 1.5 to 3 at fixed α. How does the Ackeret lift coefficient change? (√(M²−1): 1.118 and 2.828)
o: It falls by about 60%
It doubles, because the Mach number has doubled
It rises by about 60%, as the flow is faster
It stays about the same at the two Mach numbers
panel.why: C_L ∝ 1/√(M²−1): 1/2.828 versus 1/1.118 gives a ratio of 0.395, a drop of about 60%.

panel.q: Why does a supercritical airfoil reduce wave drag?
o: A flatter top weakens the shock and delays drag rise
It removes the shock entirely at all speeds above M 0.5
It increases the thickness only and nothing else
It adds a second small wing above the main one
panel.why: Flatter upper surface avoids the strong suction peak that creates a strong shock.

panel.q: Why does the sonic boom 'carpet' follow an aircraft along its ground track?
panel.model: The aircraft continuously carries its Mach cone with it, so the shock waves sweep the ground along the whole track while flight stays supersonic. Everyone along the path hears a boom as the cone passes, not only at the moment of reaching Mach 1.
panel.why: A boom is a travelling pressure signature, not a one-off event.

teach.topic: Why wings are swept and bodies are waisted
teach.model: Near the speed of sound shocks form and cause wave drag. Sweeping the wing reduces the Mach number the wing section feels, delaying the drag rise. The area rule smooths the total cross-section along the aircraft so the shocks are weaker.

How does sweep help?
What is the area rule?

stages.title: Aircraft design optimisation
stages.hook: A longer, thinner wing saves fuel but weighs more and may flutter. No single design is best in every way. How do engineers choose?
explain: Aircraft design balances conflicting requirements: aerodynamics, structure, propulsion, cost, noise and safety. Conceptual design uses sizing equations. Induced drag of a finite wing is C_Di = C_L² ÷ (π AR e), where AR is aspect ratio (b²/S) and e the span efficiency factor (about 0.8 to 0.95). Increasing AR cuts induced drag but increases structural mass.

The Breguet range equation for a jet in cruise is R = (V ÷ (g · TSFC)) (L/D) ln(W₀ ÷ W₁), where TSFC is thrust-specific fuel consumption (kg/(N·s)), W₀ the initial weight and W₁ the final weight. It shows why higher L/D, lower TSFC and a lower structural mass fraction are valuable, and the logarithm shows diminishing returns with more fuel.

Optimisation formalises the search: choose design variables (span, sweep, thickness, ...), an objective (fuel burn, cost) and constraints (stall speed, structural strength, flutter). Gradient-based methods with adjoint CFD can handle many variables. Multidisciplinary optimisation (MDO) couples aerodynamics, structures and propulsion, and when objectives conflict the result is a Pareto front of non-dominated designs.

example.q: A jet cruises at V = 250 m/s with L/D = 18, TSFC = 1.7×10⁻⁵ kg/(N·s), and W₀/W₁ = 1.25. Find the Breguet range (g = 9.81 m/s²).

analogies.city: City planners balance housing, traffic and green space; improving one can hurt another.
analogies.home: Choosing a car trades off cost, space and fuel use.
analogies.sport: A decathlete trains for many events, not just one.
analogies.tech: Phone designers trade battery size against weight.

stages.mnemonic: Many variables, one objective, strict constraints, and a Pareto front when goals conflict.
terms: Span squared divided by wing area, b²/S.
e, how close the lift distribution is to elliptical.
Cruise range from L/D, TSFC and weight fraction.
Set of designs where no objective can improve without another worsening.

misc.wrong: The optimum design is the one with the lowest drag.
misc.right: The optimum depends on the objective and constraints. Lowest drag might need a heavy, flexible wing that burns more fuel overall.

stages.limits: Closed-form sizing equations are approximate and used early in design. Optimisation results depend on the model fidelity and on the chosen constraints.

trip.prompt: Find the phases of design. What is decided in conceptual design?

questions.q: What is the main benefit of a higher aspect ratio wing?
o: Lower induced drag
Lower structural weight
Lower stall speed in all cases
Higher wave drag
questions.why: C_Di = C_L²/(π AR e) falls as AR increases.

questions.q: Why can a higher aspect ratio not be increased without limit?
o: Structural weight, flutter and airport size constraints grow
Gravity changes for long thin wings, so lift is lost
Induced drag rises as the wing gets longer and thinner
Lift disappears entirely once the ratio is large
questions.why: Long thin wings are heavier, more flexible and harder to handle on the ground.

questions.q: What does a Pareto front show?
o: Designs where improving one objective means worsening another
The cheapest design out of all the candidates only
A design that failed all the tests and was dropped
Random data points scattered with no pattern
questions.why: Points on the front are non-dominated.

questions.q: In the Breguet equation, which change increases range most directly?
o: Higher L/D
Higher TSFC
Lower cruise L/D
Lower fuel fraction
questions.why: Range is proportional to L/D and inversely to TSFC.

questions.q: A constraint in optimisation is
o: A requirement the design must satisfy, such as a stall speed limit
The quantity that the optimiser is trying to minimise
A free variable that the optimiser can change at will
An error in the calculation that must be removed
questions.why: Objective is minimised or maximised; constraints must be met.

questions.q: Induced drag coefficient C_Di = C_L²/(π AR e). With C_L = 0.8, AR = 8, e = 0.9, what is C_Di to 4 decimals?
Breguet range: V = 250 m/s, L/D = 18, TSFC = 1.7×10⁻⁵ kg/(N·s), W₀/W₁ = 1.25, g = 9.81 m/s². What is the range in km?
A wing has span 36 m and area 162 m². What is its aspect ratio b²/S?
Put these steps of an optimisation study in order.
items: Update the design using an optimiser
Check the result against higher-fidelity analysis
questions.why: The loop is set up, analysed, updated and then verified.

questions.q: Explain why increasing the wing aspect ratio reduces fuel burn but eventually stops being worthwhile.
questions.model: A higher aspect ratio reduces induced drag, which lowers fuel burn. But the wing gets heavier to carry the bending loads and may need stiffening for flutter, and the benefit shrinks since C_Di ∝ 1/AR. Eventually extra weight outweighs the drag savings, so there is an optimum.
questions.why: Design optima arise from competing trends.

panel.q: If AR is doubled at the same C_L and e, induced drag coefficient
o: Halves
Doubles
Quadruples
Stays the same
panel.why: C_Di ∝ 1/AR.

panel.q: A design is optimised for one cruise condition only. What risk does this create?
o: Poor off-design performance
Perfect performance everywhere
Reduced cost always
No risk
panel.why: Optimising a single point may degrade other conditions; multi-point optimisation avoids this.

panel.q: Why do designers use adjoint methods for aerodynamic shape optimisation?
panel.model: The adjoint method gives the gradient of an objective with respect to a very large number of shape variables at a cost close to one extra flow solution, which makes optimisation with hundreds of variables practical.
panel.why: Gradient cost is nearly independent of the number of design variables.

teach.model: A design is a balance of competing needs. A longer wing lowers induced drag but costs weight and may flutter. Engineers state an objective such as fuel burn, list constraints, and search for the best compromise, often finding a Pareto set of options.

points.ask: Why is there no single best design?
How is the search set up?
What if goals conflict?

stages.title: Flight control systems
stages.hook: A fly-by-wire jet can be flown by a pilot's gentle nudges, while computers move the surfaces hundreds of times a second. What is the computer doing in that loop?
explain: A feedback control system measures the output, compares it with the command and drives an actuator to reduce the error. A PID controller combines proportional (present error), integral (accumulated error) and derivative (rate of change of error) terms. A first-order system with time constant τ reaches 63% of a step in τ and 95% in about 3τ. A second-order system is described by natural frequency ω_n and damping ratio ζ; the overshoot is M_p = exp(−πζ/√(1−ζ²)) and the settling time to 2% is about 4/(ζω_n).

Aircraft are augmented because natural damping is often too low: stability augmentation systems feed rate gyros to control surfaces (pitch and yaw dampers), and control augmentation shapes how the aircraft responds to pilot inputs. Fly-by-wire replaces mechanical links with electrical signals and computers, adding envelope protection that limits angle of attack or load factor, and enabling relaxed static stability.

Stability of the loop is assessed with margins: gain margin and phase margin tell how much additional gain or delay the loop can tolerate before it goes unstable. Sensor noise, actuator rate limits and delays reduce margins. Safety is achieved by redundancy, monitoring, and a certification process whose aim is a very low probability of catastrophic failure per flight hour (the order of 10⁻⁹).

example.q: A pitch loop has ω_n = 4 rad/s and ζ = 0.5. Find the percent overshoot and 2% settling time.

analogies.home: A thermostat adds heat when the room is colder than set.
analogies.sport: A cyclist steers continually to hold a straight line.
analogies.sea: A ship's autopilot corrects heading errors continuously.
analogies.tech: A car cruise control raises throttle when speed drops.

terms: Controller using proportional, integral and derivative terms.
ζ, measure of how quickly oscillations die out.
Extra phase lag a loop can tolerate before instability.
Control by electrical signals through computers.
Limits that keep an aircraft within safe flight conditions.

misc.wrong: A higher feedback gain always gives better control.
misc.right: High gain improves tracking but can reduce margins and amplify noise and delays, leading to oscillation or instability.

stages.limits: Linear second-order formulas are only approximate for real nonlinear aircraft. Actual flight control law design uses gain scheduling, robust methods, and extensive testing.

trip.prompt: Find the part on flight control laws. What does envelope protection do?

questions.q: What does the integral term of a PID controller address?
o: Steady-state error that persists over time
Fast noise only, by smoothing out quick changes
Sensor failure, by switching to a backup
Nothing, because it only adds a delay
questions.why: Integral action accumulates error and drives it to zero.

stages.title: Rotorcraft performance and stability
stages.hook: A helicopter needs the most power when hovering and at high speed, but less at a moderate cruise. Where do these power demands come from?
explain: Rotor power has parts: induced power (to produce thrust), profile power (to drag the blades through the air) and parasite power (to overcome the fuselage drag), plus a small climb term. Parasite power is P_p = ½ρV³f, where f is the equivalent flat-plate area. Induced power falls with forward speed while parasite power rises as V³, so the total power curve has a minimum at a moderate speed: that speed gives best endurance; best range occurs at a higher speed where a tangent line from the origin touches the curve.

Rotor design uses non-dimensional coefficients: thrust coefficient C_T = T ÷ (ρ A (ΩR)²) and solidity σ = N_b c ÷ (π R) (blade area over disk area). The ratio C_T/σ measures blade loading and relates to stall margin. Hover ceiling falls with altitude and temperature because density falls, so more pitch is needed for the same thrust.

Stability: helicopters in hover are dynamically unstable in a slow oscillation, so pilots or stability augmentation systems hold attitude. Lateral and longitudinal modes couple through the rotor. Ground resonance can occur when blade lag motion couples with fuselage motion on the landing gear. Rotorcraft handling is governed by rotor flapping, hub design and cyclic control power.

example.q: A helicopter has equivalent flat-plate area f = 1.2 m² and flies at V = 60 m/s at sea level (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³). Find the parasite power.

stages.title: Spacecraft attitude control
stages.hook: In space there is no air to push against and no ground to hold on to. How does a satellite turn to point its camera at one spot?
explain: Attitude is the orientation of a spacecraft relative to a reference frame. Rotational motion obeys τ = I α for rotation about a principal axis, and angular momentum H = I ω is conserved if there are no external torques. Attitude can be described by Euler angles, direction cosine matrices or quaternions, which avoid the singularities of Euler angles.

Sensors determine attitude: Sun sensors, star trackers (most accurate), horizon sensors, magnetometers and gyros. Actuators change it: reaction wheels and control moment gyros exchange angular momentum with the body without using propellant, while thrusters and magnetic torquers apply external torques. A wheel with inertia I_w spinning at ω_w has H = I_w ω_w, and the spacecraft rotates the opposite way: ω_s = −I_w ω_w ÷ I_s.

External disturbance torques (gravity gradient, solar radiation pressure, aerodynamic drag in low orbit, magnetic) slowly build up angular momentum in the wheels until they saturate. A momentum dump uses thrusters or magnetorquers to remove it. A rest-to-rest slew with constant torque τ and accelerate/decelerate halves takes t = 2√(θ I ÷ τ). Spin stabilisation and gravity-gradient booms are passive options.

example.q: A spacecraft (I = 120 kg·m²) uses a torque of 0.6 N·m to slew by 0.9 rad, accelerating for half the time and decelerating for the rest. How long does it take?
steps: Each half covers θ/2 = 0.45 rad = ½ α (t/2)², so (t/2)² = 0.9 ÷ 0.005 = 180.

stages.title: Spacecraft thermal and power systems
stages.hook: A satellite in sunlight can be too hot and in Earth's shadow too cold, and it can only lose heat by radiating it. How is its temperature kept within limits?
explain: In vacuum, heat leaves only by radiation, following the Stefan-Boltzmann law: P = ε σ A T⁴, with σ = 5.67×10⁻⁸ W/(m²·K⁴). A simple sphere in sunlight absorbs α S π r² (solar constant S = 1361 W/m² at 1 AU) and radiates ε σ T⁴ 4π r². If α = ε, the equilibrium temperature is T = (S ÷ (4σ))^¼ ≈ 278 K. Real spacecraft choose coatings: the ratio α/ε sets temperature. Thermal control uses multi-layer insulation, radiators, heaters, heat pipes and louvres.

Power usually comes from solar arrays, with power P = η S A cos θ where θ is the angle between the Sun and the array normal. Cells have efficiency about 30% for multi-junction types and degrade over time from radiation. Batteries carry the spacecraft through eclipse. The capacity must account for depth of discharge: C = P t ÷ DoD. Solar flux falls with distance as 1/d², so outer-planet missions use radioisotope thermoelectric generators instead.

Power and thermal design are coupled: all electrical power ends up as heat that must be radiated. The design is sized for hot and cold cases, such as peak sun with maximum dissipation versus eclipse with minimum dissipation. Missions to Venus and Mercury face hot extremes, and those to Jupiter and beyond face low light.

stages.title: Launch vehicle engineering
stages.hook: Why do nearly all orbital rockets have two or three stages when a single big stage would seem simpler?
explain: A launch vehicle must supply roughly 9 to 9.5 km/s of Δv to reach low Earth orbit, including losses to gravity and drag. The rocket equation Δv = v_e ln(m₀/m_f) shows that a single stage with an achievable structural fraction (about 0.08 to 0.12) and chemical propellants would barely reach orbit with no payload. Staging allows each stage to shed its dead mass. For a stage with structural coefficient ε = m_s/(m_s + m_p) and payload ratio λ, Δv = v_e ln((1 + λ)/(ε + λ)).

Lift-off requires thrust-to-weight above 1, typically 1.2 to 1.5 for orbital launchers. The vehicle experiences maximum dynamic pressure q = ½ρv² (max-Q) about a minute into flight, at an altitude near the tropopause region, where aerodynamic loads peak. Engine cycles include gas-generator and staged-combustion, differing in efficiency and complexity. Vehicle structure is a thin-walled tank structure with the tanks pressurised to carry compressive loads, and mass margin is vital.

Engineering also covers trajectory (a gravity turn, then circularisation), guidance and control (thrust vector control, gimballed engines), pogo oscillation, propellant slosh, ground operations and safety, and reusability: recovering a stage saves hardware cost but needs reserve propellant for landing. Launch sites near the equator gain Earth-rotation speed (up to about 0.46 km/s).

example.q: A stage has Isp = 300 s (v_e = 2943 m/s), structural coefficient ε = 0.10 and payload ratio λ = 0.05. Find its Δv.
